items.stem: Write some uses of metals which are based on the properties of malleability and ductility.
items.answer: (i) Silver foils are used for decorative purposes on sweets. (ii) Aluminium foils are used for wrapping chocolates, food stuff, etc. (iii) Thin copper wires are used in electric circuits. (iv) Gold and silver ornaments are made into different designs.

items.stem: Define the term 'electrical conductivity of metals'. Arrange the following metals in order of their decreasing electrical conductivity. Or Give reason why metals conduct electricity.
items.answer: (i) The free flow of electrons in metals, i.e., the property of conductivity of electric current in metals is called electrical conductivity. These metals offer little resistance to the flow of current. (ii) Silver is the best conductor of electricity followed by gold. Mercury comes at last.
items.ocr: Printed stem opens the quotation ('electrical conductivity of metals) but never closes it; closing quote restored. The list of metals the question asks you to arrange was not captured by MinerU - the answer shows it ran silver > gold > ... > mercury. The lower-case 'or' in the printed stem introduces the alternative wording of the same question and has been kept.

items.stem: Why are cooking vessels and water boilers generally made of copper and aluminium?
items.answer: Cooking vessels and water boilers are generally made of copper and aluminium because they are good conductors of heat. Hence, the cooking vessels and boilers will get heated up quickly.
items.ocr: Stripped the advertising line 'Click Here to Buy book on Amazon' and the '## Page 18' marker that follow this item.

items.stem: How does a metal conduct heat?
items.answer: Atoms of a metal gain energy when heated and vibrate more vigorously. This energy is transferred to the electrons which move through the metal. They in turn transfer their energy to other electrons and atoms, and thus heat is conducted.

items.stem: What properties do you think of while categorizing elements as metals and non-metals?
items.answer: We consider various physical properties like lustre, sonority, malleability, ductility, etc. We also consider chemical properties like reaction with oxygen, water, etc.
items.ocr: Printed 'lustre sonority' with no comma; comma restored for readability.

items.stem: Why are metals said to be electro-positive?
items.answer:
Metals are electro-positive because they ionise by loss of electrons and form positive ions.
Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
Ca → Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻
items.ocr: MinerU dropped both reaction arrows and printed them as stray '$' signs ('Na $ Na+ + eCa $ Ca2+ + 2e'), which also ran the two equations together; arrows restored as →, the equations separated and the electron charges restored as e⁻.

items.stem: Some metals do not get oxidised. Why?
items.answer: The surface of metals like Mg, Al, Zn, Pb, etc. gets covered with a thin layer of oxide. This layer prevents the metal from further oxidation.

items.stem: What happens when a metal reacts with dilute acid?
items.answer:
Metal salt is formed and hydrogen gas is evolved.
Metal + dilute acid → Metal salt + Hydrogen
e.g., Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
items.ocr: The word-equation arrow was lost and printed as a stray '$' ('Metal + dilute acid $ Metal salt + Hydrogen'); restored as →. LaTeX chemistry rewritten to Unicode subscripts.

items.stem: Why do metals generally not form compounds with hydrogen?
items.answer: This is because metals form compounds by the loss of electrons, which are accepted by the other element. But hydrogen usually forms compounds with other elements either by the loss of electrons or by sharing of electrons. It does not accept electrons.

items.stem: Sodium or potassium pieces should not be thrown into a sink in the laboratory. Why?
items.answer: Both sodium and potassium react vigorously with air and water. The reaction is highly exothermic and the evolved gas may even catch fire.
items.ocr: Stem printed 'thrown into a sink the laboratory' - the preposition 'in' was dropped and has been restored. The answer printed 'Both sodium and potassium pieces vigorously with air and water', losing its verb; 'react' restored and the redundant 'pieces' dropped.

items.stem: Hydrogen is a non-metal, still it is given a place in the reactivity series. Why?
items.answer: The reactivity of metals depends on how easily they can lose electrons. Like metals, hydrogen also loses electrons and forms positive ions. Hence, it is placed in the reactivity series.

items.stem: Aluminium occurs in combined state whereas gold is found in free state. Why?
items.answer: Aluminium is a more reactive metal, it reacts with air, water and acid, while gold is the least reactive metal, it does not react with air, water or acid.

items.stem: Why do surfaces of aluminium vessels acquire a dull appearance when exposed to air?
items.answer: Surface of aluminium vessels becomes dull due to formation of a layer of aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) when it is exposed to air.
items.ocr: LaTeX '\left(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\right)' rewritten to Al₂O₃.

items.stem: A substance X, which is an oxide of a metal, is used intensively in the cement industry. This element is present in bones also. On treatment with water it forms a solution which turns red litmus blue. Identify X and also write the chemical reactions involved.
items.answer:
X is calcium oxide (CaO).
CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq)

items.answer:
(i) Hydrogen gas. (Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂↑)
(ii) Downward displacement of water.
(iii) Insoluble in water.
(iv) Lighter than air.

items.stem: A metal A, which is used in thermit process, when heated with oxygen gives an oxide B, which is amphoteric in nature. Identify A and B. Write down the reactions of oxide B with HCl and NaOH.
items.answer:
A is aluminium (Al) and B is aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃).
Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O
Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O

items.answer:
When zinc reacts with dil. sulphuric acid, bubbles of hydrogen are seen to come out.
Zn + dil. H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂↑

items.stem:
(a) Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu
(b) Cu + FeSO₄ → CuSO₄ + Fe
Which of the above two reactions will take place and why?
items.answer: Reaction (a) will take place. This is because Fe is more reactive than copper and so, it can displace Cu from its compound CuSO₄.

items.stem: Explain why most of the metals do not displace hydrogen from nitric acid.
items.answer: Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent. It oxidises the hydrogen produced to water and itself gets reduced to the nitrogen oxides.

items.stem: When a metal X is treated with cold water, it gives a base Y with molecular formula XOH (Molecular mass = 40) and liberates a gas Z which easily catches fire. Identify X, Y and Z and also write the reaction involved.
items.answer:
X is sodium (Na), Y is sodium hydroxide (NaOH), Z is hydrogen (H₂).
2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) + Heat energy

items.stem: Why do the articles made of aluminium not corrode?
items.answer: The articles made of aluminium do not corrode because on exposure to air, the surface of aluminium is coated with a thin layer of aluminium oxide which is non-reactive. This protective layer protects the metal underneath from further damage.

items.stem: What are the constituents of solder alloy? Which property of solder makes it suitable for welding electrical wires?
items.answer: Solder is an alloy of lead and tin. Low melting point of solder makes it suitable for welding electrical wires.

items.stem:
(i) Select a metal out of the following which reacts with hot water but not with cold water : Iron, sodium, magnesium.
(ii) Write the chemical equation of the reaction and name the main product formed during this reaction.
items.answer:
(i) Metal is iron.
(ii) 3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) —Heat→ Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)
The main product formed is iron oxide, Fe₃O₄.

items.stem: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity in molten state?
items.answer: In solid state, ionic compounds do not conduct electric current because the ions are held together in fixed positions by strong electrostatic forces and cannot move freely. When ionic solid is dissolved in water or melted, the crystal structure is broken down and ions become free to move and conduct electricity.

items.stem: How are the less reactive metals extracted? Explain with the help of an example.
items.answer:
Metals low in the reactivity series are very less reactive. The oxides of these metals can be reduced to metals by heating alone. For example, cinnabar (HgS) is an ore of mercury. When it is heated in air (roasted) it is first converted into mercuric oxide (HgO). Mercuric oxide is then reduced to mercury on further heating.
2HgS(s) + 3O₂(g) —Heat→ 2HgO(s) + 2SO₂(g)
2HgO(s) —Heat→ 2Hg(l) + O₂(g)

items.stem: Name two metals that catch fire when put in water and why?
items.answer: Sodium and potassium. Sodium and potassium are highly electropositive metals which react vigorously with cold water to evolve hydrogen gas. The reaction is highly violent and exothermic and the evolved gas catches fire.
items.ocr: The printed answer reads 'highly negative metal', which contradicts the chapter (and item 92, which establishes that metals are electro-positive); read as 'electropositive' and pluralised. Source defect recorded.

items.stem: What would you observe when zinc is added to a solution of iron(II) sulphate? Write the chemical reaction that takes place.
items.answer:
The pale green colour of iron(II) sulphate will fade and a colourless solution of ZnSO₄ will be obtained. Greyish particles of Fe are also formed.
Zn(s) + FeSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Fe(s) [greyish]

items.stem: Name two metals that start floating after sometime when immersed in water and why?
items.answer: Calcium and magnesium. Calcium and magnesium react with cold and hot water to evolve hydrogen gas. The bubbles of the gas evolved stick to the surface of the metal and thus, being lighter, it floats on the surface.

items.stem: Metal oxides are basic in nature. But some metal oxides show both acidic as well as basic behaviour. What are these oxides called? Name one such oxide and write the reaction with an acid and a base.
items.answer: Oxides which show acidic as well as basic behaviour are called amphoteric oxides. Example : aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.

items.stem: An element reacts with air (oxygen) to form its oxide. When dissolved in water the solution turns red litmus blue. Is it a metal or a non-metal? Justify your answer.
items.answer:
A basic oxide turns red litmus blue, so it is a metallic oxide. Hence the element is a metal. e.g.,
Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH
MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂

items.stem: List any two observations when a highly reactive metal is dropped in water.
items.answer: (i) Large amount of heat is evolved. (ii) Metal starts floating.

items.stem:
(a) Name a metal for each case : (i) It does not react with cold as well as hot water but reacts with steam. (ii) [second case not printed]
(b) When calcium metal is added to water the gas evolved does not catch fire but the same gas evolved on adding sodium metal to water catches fire. Why is it so?
items.answer:
(a) (i) Aluminium, (ii) Copper.
(b) In both cases, the gas evolved is H₂. When calcium reacts with water the heat evolved is not sufficient for hydrogen to catch fire. On the other hand, sodium metal reacts with water violently and in this case a lot of heat is evolved which is sufficient for hydrogen to catch fire.

items.stem: Give reasons for the following : (a) Sodium chloride has a high melting point. (b) Non-metals do not displace hydrogen from dilute acids.
items.answer:
(a) Sodium chloride does not exist as a molecule but as aggregates of oppositely charged ions which are held tightly by strong electrostatic force. This is why we need high temperature to break this force of attraction between ions and hence it has a high melting point.
(b) Non-metals have less reactivity than hydrogen, so they cannot displace hydrogen from dilute acids.

items.stem: Explain how mercury is extracted from its sulphide ore (Cinnabar). Give equations of the reactions involved.
items.answer:
When cinnabar is heated in air, it is first converted into mercuric oxide (HgO). Mercuric oxide is then reduced on further heating.
2HgS(s) + 3O₂(g) —Heat→ 2HgO(s) + 2SO₂(g)
2HgO(s) —Heat→ 2Hg(l) + O₂(g)

items.stem: In one method of rust prevention, the iron is not coated with anything. Name the method and define it.
items.answer: Electrical protection (cathodic / sacrificial protection) : The method is used for protecting iron articles which are in contact with each other, i.e., underground pipes. The iron article is connected to more reactive metals, i.e., magnesium and zinc. Therefore, Mg will be corroded and it will protect iron from being rusted.

items.stem: State reasons for the following : (i) Silver chloride becomes black after sometime when exposed to air. (ii) Although aluminium is a highly reactive metal, yet its articles do not corrode.
items.answer:
(i) Silver chloride becomes black after sometime when exposed to air as it reacts with sulphur in air to form a black coating of silver sulphide.
(ii) Although aluminium is a highly reactive metal, yet its articles do not corrode due to the formation of a protective layer of oxide, Al₂O₃, on its surface which prevents it from further corrosion.

items.stem: Name the constituents of bronze and write its two uses.
items.answer:
Constituents of bronze are Copper + Zinc.
Uses of bronze : (i) Used for making coins. (ii) Used for making turbines and blades.

items.stem: Explain how the properties of an alloy are different from those of constituent metals.
items.answer: Properties of alloys differ from those of the constituent metals in respect of hardness, strength and resistance to corrosion, which are increased, while melting point, malleability and conductivity are decreased.
items.ocr: Printed answer is ungrammatical ('in respect of hardness, strongness, resistant to corrosion, which is increased while melting point, malleable and conductivity decreased'); the noun forms have been regularised without changing the claim.

items.stem: Why is sodium kept immersed in kerosene oil?
items.answer: Sodium reacts so vigorously with the oxygen of air that it catches fire if kept in the open. Sodium is kept immersed in kerosene oil to protect it from the action of air and moisture and to prevent accidental fires.

items.stem: Give reason : (i) Why do aluminium sheets not corrode easily? (ii) Why is a copper vessel covered with a green coating in rainy season?
items.answer:
(i) Aluminium does not corrode easily because on exposure to air, its surface is coated with a thin layer of aluminium oxide which is protective and non-reactive.
(ii) It is because copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide in the air and slowly loses its shiny brown surface and gains a green coat.

items.stem: Explain why sodium hydroxide solution cannot be kept in aluminium containers. Write the equation for the reaction that may take place.
items.answer:
Aluminium is an amphoteric metal. It reacts with NaOH to form NaAlO₂ (sodium aluminate). So, NaOH cannot be stored in an aluminium container.
2Al + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂(g)

The name gloss '(sodium aluminate)' after NaAlO₂ is supplied, not transcribed.

items.stem: What are the electron dot structures of magnesium and chlorine? Show the formation of magnesium chloride by the transfer of electrons.
items.answer:
Magnesium (2, 8, 2) has two valence electrons and chlorine (2, 8, 7) has seven. Magnesium loses its two valence electrons and each of two chlorine atoms gains one, so that all three attain a stable octet :
Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
2Cl + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻
Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → MgCl₂
The Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are then held together by strong electrostatic attraction in magnesium chloride, MgCl₂.

The printed stem reads 'What is electron dot structures ... and show the formation', which has been split into two sentences.

items.stem: Give reasons for the following : (a) We can store copper sulphate solution in a silver vessel but not silver nitrate solution in a copper vessel. (b) Food cans are coated with tin rather than zinc.
items.answer:
(a) We can store copper sulphate solution in a silver vessel, because silver is less reactive than copper. So, displacement reaction does not occur. But we cannot store silver nitrate in a copper container because copper is more reactive than silver. So, it displaces silver from its salt.
Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag
(b) Tin is a less reactive metal than zinc. So, it is not easily attacked by components of food items.

items.stem: What happens when magnesium ribbon is burnt in air? What is the state of the metal oxide in the product formed?
items.answer:
When magnesium ribbon is burnt in air, it burns with a dazzling light and a white coloured magnesium oxide is formed, which is a solid (a white powder).
2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)

items.stem: A metal X combines with a non-metal Y by the transfer of electrons to form a compound Z. (i) State the type of bond in compound Z. (ii) What can you say about the melting and boiling point of compound Z? (iii) Will this compound dissolve in kerosene or petrol? (iv) Will this compound be a good conductor of electricity?
items.answer:
(i) Ionic bond in compound Z.
(ii) It has high melting and boiling point due to stronger inter-ionic attraction.
(iii) No, as electrovalent compounds are soluble in water but insoluble in kerosene or petrol.
(iv) No, as its solution in water contains ions but in solid state it does not conduct electricity, as movement of ions is not possible due to its rigid structure.

items.stem: What prevents the metals such as magnesium, aluminium, zinc and lead from oxidation at ordinary temperature?
items.answer: At ordinary temperature, the surfaces of metals such as magnesium, aluminium, zinc and lead, etc., are covered with a thin layer of oxide. The protective oxide layer prevents the metals from further oxidation.

items.stem: What is meant by galvanisation? Why is it done?
items.answer: The process of depositing a thin layer of zinc metal on iron objects is called galvanisation. Galvanisation is done to protect the iron objects from rusting. This is because zinc metal does not corrode on exposure to damp air (due to the presence of a thin zinc oxide layer on its surface).
